passage: Playgroup note, Thursday, from Uma. Nikita (2 years) rubbed her eyes twice during story time and slumped against my knee. When I asked, "Sleepy?" she nodded and pointed to the nap mats. Before lunch she patted her tummy and said, "Hungry, khana." After lunch she tugged at her shorts and did a little dance; we reached the potty just in time. 👍 I'll tell her father she's starting to put words to what her body feels.

qa.q: Where did Nikita point when asked if she was sleepy?
qa.a: To the nap mats.

qa.q: What does Nikita patting her tummy and saying "khana" show she understood?
qa.a: It shows she noticed the hungry feeling inside her and wanted food.

qa.q: What could Nikita's father do at home to build on this?
qa.a: He could name her body feelings in simple words, like sleepy or hungry, and respond when she signals them.

qa.q: How might Uma's day change as Nikita names her needs?
qa.a: Uma can meet Nikita's needs sooner, with fewer meltdowns and fewer accidents. 🙂

grounding: Shows a toddler noticing and signalling tiredness, hunger and the need for the toilet.

passage: On the local bus home from the weekly haat, Aparna, two, stops chattering. She pulls at her sandal strap and whimpers, then pushes her face into Bidisha's sari. Her mother loosens the strap; a red line shows on the small foot. Aparna sighs, then yawns wide and curls up in Bidisha's lap. By the next stop she is asleep, one fist still holding a paper packet of roasted chana.

qa.q: What mark did Bidisha find on Aparna's foot?
qa.a: A red line from the sandal strap.

qa.q: Why did Aparna whimper and pull at her sandal?
qa.a: The strap was hurting and she was tired, and she wanted the discomfort to stop.

qa.q: What could Bidisha try after this trip?
qa.a: She could check how the sandals fit and plan a rest before long outings, while watching for these signals.

qa.q: What would change if Bidisha had scolded Aparna for fussing?
qa.a: The signal about the strap might have been missed, and Aparna could have stayed sore and cried harder.

grounding: Shows a toddler signalling physical discomfort and tiredness on a village bus ride.

passage: At the playground in Leeds, Tariq, nearly three, stops halfway up the climbing frame and grabs the front of his trousers. "Wee-wee," he says, climbing down fast. Fatima, his mother, takes his hand and they hurry to the cafe toilet. Back outside, he shivers and holds out his arms. "Cold." She zips up his coat. He nods, pats the zip, and runs back to the frame.

qa.q: Which word did Tariq use when he felt cold?
qa.a: He said "Cold."

qa.q: Why did Tariq climb down so fast?
qa.a: He felt he needed to wee and wanted to reach the toilet in time.

qa.q: What went right, and how could Fatima keep it going?
qa.a: Tariq named his need early; she can keep responding quickly and noticing when he tells her.

qa.q: What is it like for Fatima when Tariq can say what his body needs?
qa.a: Outings feel easier and calmer because she doesn't have to guess.

grounding: Shows a toddler recognising the need for the toilet and feeling cold, and telling his mother.

passage: I'm Neelam, Seema's grandmother. At two, Seema has started telling us about her body. This morning she stopped playing, tugged at her nappy and said, "Wet." At lunch she pushed her plate away and rubbed her eyes. "Sleepy," she whispered, and crawled onto my lap. Later she held her tummy and made a face. I checked; she needed the toilet. She is learning what her body is saying.

qa.q: What did Seema say when she tugged at her nappy?
qa.a: She said, "Wet."

qa.q: What did Seema's rubbing her eyes and whispering "Sleepy" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt tired and knew she needed rest.

qa.q: How can Neelam support Seema in noticing her body signals?
qa.a: By naming the feelings back to her and responding quickly, like helping her rest or go to the toilet.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Seema's new words?
qa.a: Neelam sees them as Seema learning to understand what her body is telling her. 😊

grounding: Shows a grandmother noticing a toddler recognising and naming hunger, tiredness and toilet needs.

passage:
Tuesday: Abhinav, twenty months, whines and throws his toy car. His father Chinmay tries to play, but Abhinav cries louder.

Thursday: Abhinav whines again at the same time. Chinmay asks, "Hungry?" Abhinav points to the kitchen.

The next Monday: Before lunch, Abhinav walks to the kitchen, pats his tummy and says, "Eat!" Chinmay smiles and hands him a banana.

qa.q: What did Abhinav say on Monday before lunch?
qa.a: He said, "Eat!"

qa.q: What was Abhinav likely feeling when he whined and threw his car on Tuesday?
qa.a: He was likely hungry and upset but didn't know how to show it yet.

qa.q: What helped Abhinav connect his feeling to food?
qa.a: His father asking "Hungry?" helped him link the uncomfortable feeling to eating.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel on Monday when Abhinav says "Eat!"?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy that Abhinav can now tell him what he needs.

grounding: Shows a toddler over several days learning to recognise hunger and say what he needs.

passage: Keerthana stopped in the middle of the building's play area, crossed her legs and went very still. Her uncle Saurabh, visiting from Pune, didn't notice at first. "Susu," she said, tugging his kurta. "Susu now!" He grabbed her hand and ran for the lift. They made it, just. Back downstairs, she yawned, rubbed her eyes with both fists and climbed into his lap, the swing forgotten.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say while tugging Saurabh's kurta?
qa.a: She said, "Susu now!"

qa.q: What does Keerthana rubbing her eyes and climbing into Saurabh's lap suggest?
qa.a: She was tired and wanted comfort; her body's signals mattered more to her than the swing.

qa.q: What could Saurabh watch for next time he looks after Keerthana?
qa.a: Early signs like crossing her legs or going still, so he can take her to the toilet before it becomes urgent.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel after the rush to the lift?
qa.a: Relieved they made it in time, and maybe surprised at how clearly she told him what she needed.

grounding: Shows a toddler noticing and naming the need to use the toilet and later showing tiredness.

passage:
"Tummy," Vikas said, pressing his hand flat on his shirt.
"Your tummy hurts?" Vandana asked, putting down her laptop.
"No. Tummy empty."
She laughed. "Empty! You mean hungry?"
"Hungry. Banana."
"You had lunch an hour ago."
"Banana, Mummy." He leaned on her knee, eyes half shut.
"Hungry and sleepy, both?" she said. "Half a banana, then nap."
He ate it in four bites and was asleep on the mat before she had dropped the peel in the bin.

qa.q: What did Vikas ask for?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: How can you tell that Vikas felt tired as well as hungry?
qa.a: He leaned on her knee with his eyes half shut and fell asleep right after eating, so he was sleepy and worn out.

qa.q: What did Vandana do well when Vikas said "tummy"?
qa.a: She stopped to ask what he meant instead of guessing, which helped him find the right word, hungry.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had refused the banana because lunch was recent?
qa.a: Vikas might have got upset and cranky, and he would learn that telling her his body's signals doesn't help.

grounding: Shows a toddler noticing hunger and tiredness in his body and finding words for them with his mother's help.

passage:
Creche note from Payal, a hot afternoon in May
Mehak came in from the shaded yard with red cheeks and went straight to the water jug, patting it and saying "paani, paani." She drank a full cup. After lunch she pulled at her dress and said "hot." I changed her into a cotton frock and put her mat under the fan. She was asleep in minutes. I've told her mother she is naming more of what her body feels now 😊

qa.q: What did Mehak say while patting the water jug?
qa.a: She said "paani, paani."

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she pulled at her dress and said "hot"?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and too warm, and she wanted Payal to fix it.

qa.q: How could Payal keep supporting Mehak's naming of body signals?
qa.a: Keep answering quickly when Mehak names a need, and give her words for new signals like "thirsty" or "sleepy".

qa.q: How might Mehak's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: Glad and reassured that Mehak is learning to tell carers what her body needs.

grounding: Shows a toddler recognising thirst, heat and tiredness on a summer day, noted by her carer.

passage: Winter in their village near Mandi meant layers: woollen pyjamas, socks, a thick sweater. Sumit, two, was playing with pine cones on the sunny steps when he suddenly stopped, tugged at the waist of his pyjamas, and wriggled. "Su-su!" he shouted. His mother, Vidya, dropped the washing and ran him to the bathroom. They made it, just. "You told me! Well done." Sumit looked very serious, then went back to his pine cones.

qa.q: What was Sumit playing with?
qa.a: Pine cones on the sunny steps.

qa.q: What does Sumit's serious look afterwards suggest?
qa.a: Sumit seemed proud and a little surprised that telling his mother worked.

qa.q: How could Vidya help Sumit keep noticing this signal in winter?
qa.a: She could dress him in pyjamas that pull down easily and keep praising him for telling her early.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel after they made it in time?
qa.a: Vidya probably felt relieved and pleased, seeing Sumit notice and name the signal.

grounding: On a winter day in a Himachal village, a toddler notices his need for the toilet and tells his mother.

passage: During the June street festival in Lisbon, the whole neighbourhood smelled of grilled sardines, and music played till late. Sofia, two, danced on her mother's feet until almost ten. Then she stopped, rubbed her eyes, and pulled at Beatriz's skirt. "Cama," she said. "Bed." Beatriz knelt. "You're tired?" Sofia nodded and leaned her head on her mother's shoulder. Beatriz carried her home under the paper garlands, and Sofia was asleep before the second corner.

qa.q: What did the neighbourhood smell of?
qa.a: Grilled sardines.

qa.q: How was Sofia feeling when she said 'Cama'?
qa.a: Sofia felt tired and sleepy, and knew she needed to rest.

qa.q: Why was it good that Beatriz asked 'You're tired?'
qa.a: It named the feeling for Sofia, helping her link the body signal to the word.

qa.q: How might Beatriz feel carrying Sofia home?
qa.a: Beatriz probably felt tender and glad that Sofia could tell her she was tired.

grounding: At a summer street festival in Portugal, a toddler notices her tiredness and asks for bed.

passage: I'm Pradeep, Lavanya's uncle. At our Onam lunch, the sadya took forever to be served. Lavanya, not quite two, was fine for the first hour. Then she stopped patting the flower pookalam, came to me, patted her tummy and said, "Mum-mum." She opened her mouth like a little bird. I don't know if she was really hungry or had just seen the payasam. But I gave her a bit of banana from the leaf, and she stopped fussing at once.

qa.q: What did Pradeep give Lavanya from the leaf?
qa.a: A bit of banana.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have been feeling when she patted her tummy?
qa.a: Lavanya was probably hungry and impatient after the long wait.

qa.q: How could adults help Lavanya connect her tummy signal to eating?
qa.a: Respond to her 'mum-mum' quickly and name it, 'You're hungry', so she learns the signal works.

qa.q: How does Pradeep read Lavanya's signal?
qa.a: Pradeep isn't sure whether she was hungry or had just seen the payasam, but responds kindly and notices she settles.

grounding: An uncle describes a toddler signalling hunger during a long Onam lunch.

passage:
First week of Onam holidays: Jomon squats behind the sofa and wets his shorts. Ganga cleans him up and says, "Next time, tell Amma."

Four days later: in the middle of playing, he stops, grabs the front of his shorts and looks at Ganga. She takes him to the potty, just in time.

Thiruvonam morning, in his new mundu: "Amma, soo-soo!" Ganga laughs and runs with him.

qa.q: What did Jomon say on Thiruvonam morning?
qa.a: He said, "Amma, soo-soo!"

qa.q: How did Ganga likely feel on Thiruvonam morning?
qa.a: Ganga was probably delighted and relieved, laughing as she ran with Jomon.

qa.q: How did Ganga support Jomon in noticing his body's signal?
qa.a: She stayed calm after the accident, gave him simple words to use, and responded quickly when he signalled.

qa.q: What might Jomon feel when Ganga responds quickly to his signal?
qa.a: Jomon may feel proud and understood, which helps him keep telling her.

grounding: Over the Onam holidays, a toddler moves from not noticing his need to pee to signalling it with a gesture and then words.

passage:
During Ramzan, the evenings in the Hyderabad flat were loud with guests arriving for iftar. By eight, Yusuf, two, was rubbing his eyes and pulling at his ear.

Gurpreet Aunty from next door tried to give him a sweet. He pushed it away and flopped on the carpet, whining.

His mother noticed. "He's not hungry, he's sleepy," she said, and carried him to the quiet bedroom. Within minutes he was asleep.

qa.q: What was Yusuf doing by eight?
qa.a: He was rubbing his eyes and pulling at his ear.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he pushed away the sweet and whined?
qa.a: Yusuf was tired and cranky, overwhelmed by the noise and ready to sleep.

qa.q: How did Yusuf's mother respond well to his signals?
qa.a: She read the eye-rubbing and whining as tiredness, not hunger, and took him somewhere quiet to sleep.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet Aunty have understood Yusuf's whining?
qa.a: Gurpreet Aunty may have thought he wanted a treat, and then learned it was tiredness when his mother explained.

grounding: During busy Ramzan evenings, a toddler shows tiredness through body signals and his mother recognises them.

passage:
"Manoj, why is she hitting her tummy?" Ganga asked.

Their daughter Chinni stood by the fridge in the May heat, patting her stomach and saying, "Ow."

"It's two hours since lunch," Manoj said. "Hungry?"

"Chinni, are you hungry?"

Chinni nodded hard and pointed at the fridge.

Ganga gave her a slice of watermelon. Chinni ate it, then patted her tummy again and smiled. "Ow gone."

Manoj laughed. "She's learning what her tummy is telling her."

qa.q: What did Ganga give Chinni?
qa.a: Ganga gave her a slice of watermelon.

qa.q: How did Chinni feel after eating the watermelon?
qa.a: Chinni seemed satisfied and happy, smiling and saying "Ow gone".

qa.q: How did Manoj and Ganga help Chinni understand her body signal?
qa.a: They noticed her gesture, asked a simple question, and responded quickly, so she linked the feeling to hunger.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel about Chinni's words?
qa.a: Manoj was amused and pleased, seeing that she was learning what her tummy was telling her.

grounding: In the summer heat, a toddler signals hunger by patting her tummy, and her parents help her connect the feeling with food.

passage:
Note for Ojas's Papa, from Nani, Saturday
Before lunch Ojas patted his tummy and said "mum-mum", so he knows when he's hungry now. After lunch he rubbed his eyes and dragged his blanket to me, and he went down for his nap without a fuss. Earlier he'd stopped playing, held his nappy and fussed; he needed changing. His cousin Suraj kept wanting to play trains and sulked when Ojas lay down, so I let Suraj choose the nap-time story. 🙂

qa.q: What did Ojas drag to Nani after lunch?
qa.a: He dragged his blanket to her.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he rubbed his eyes?
qa.a: He was tired and sleepy, and bringing his blanket showed he knew he wanted rest.

qa.q: How could Nani keep helping Ojas notice his body's signals?
qa.a: She could name each signal out loud, like "you're hungry" or "you're sleepy", whenever he shows it.

qa.q: What is it like for Suraj when Ojas lies down for his nap?
qa.a: Suraj feels disappointed to lose a playmate, but choosing the story helps Suraj feel included.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler beginning to recognise hunger, tiredness and a wet nappy and signal them to a caregiver.
